questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14062909/assets/2f08e0a0d1fd855f2d179ac65dbdf5d022f3488b85c78b5cbb507f12bd69487e.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(-1,1)$ and has a radius of $1,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-(-1))^{2}+(y-1)^{2}={1}^{2}\,⟹\,(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+1)^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y-1)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2(x+1)+2(y-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2(x+1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{y-1} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+1}{1-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(-3,-2)$ and has a radius of $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-(-3))^{2}+(y-(-2))^{2}={2}^{2}\,⟹\,(x+3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=4.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+3)^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y+2)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2(x+3)+2(y+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2(x+3) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+3}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since our circle is centered at $(0,-2)$ and has a radius of $3,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-0)^{2}+(y-(-2))^{2}={3}^{2}\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=9.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+(y+2)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y+2)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2(y+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since our circle is centered at the origin and has a radius of $4,$ its equation is given by

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={4}^{2}\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(16) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at the origin and has semiaxes $1$ and $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ 2x+\frac{2y}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the right-opening parabola shown above. Express the answer in terms of the variable $y.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola has its vertex at $O,$ and passes through the point $(5,7).$

The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Substituting $x=5$ and $y=7$ into the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(7)^{2} & =4p(5) \\ 49 & =20p \\ p & =\frac{49}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of our parabola is 

$$
{y}^{2}=\frac{49}{5}x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{49}{5}x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{49}{5} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{49}{10y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(0,-1)$ and has a radius of $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-0)^2 + (y - (-1))^2 = 2^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + (y+1)^2 = 4.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y+1)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2(y+1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y+1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y+1}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

y^2 = \dfrac{4}{3}x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{3}x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$
